tagline.text: A sea turtle hatchery in Morong run by former poachers turned protectors

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,200 (day trip from Manila including round-trip transport, per person)

children.text: Since 1999 the Pawikan Conservation Center on the Nagbalayong coast of Morong, Bataan, has been protecting olive ridley sea turtle eggs and returning hatchlings to the sea, run by the local community. You can tour the hatchery and release a hatchling yourself, which makes it a good stop with children.

The Pawikan Conservation Center sits on the beach in the village of Nagbalayong in Morong, Bataan. "Pawikan" is the Tagalog word for sea turtle. This coast is a long-established nesting ground where sea turtles come ashore to lay eggs, and the center is run by a local people's group, Bantay Pawikan, Inc. It is a remote coastal village that lies farther toward the sea to the west of Morong, about
175 km
from Manila by road.

What makes the center special is that the people who run it once collected and sold turtle eggs themselves. A local notice says they have now become the turtles' guardians. According to one travel account, the village agreed to stop collecting eggs after a United Nations representative explained the threat of extinction, and the Japanese government later provided long fishnets called "baklad" so former egg gatherers could work as fishermen and turtle protectors. The center began in 1999 as a community-based program to rescue, rehabilitate, protect and propagate sea turtles.

On a visit you first hear a lecture about the turtle life cycle and the center's work, then see the fenced hatchery where eggs collected from the beach are buried and a turtle-shaped concrete pool where hatchlings are held. If the timing is right, staff will guide you to carry hatchlings to the water's edge and release them. Three of the five sea turtle species found in the Philippines (hawksbill, olive ridley and green turtle) are said to nest around Morong and Bagac.

The turtles you see here are mainly olive ridleys, which local material describes as endangered. The Bataan tourism office explains that nesting on the beach runs from September to January and the center secures the eggs laid during that period. Not every hatchling grows up, though. One visitor explains that only a small fraction of the hatchlings that reach the sea become adults, and the surviving females return to lay eggs on the beach where they were born. It is less a tourist attraction than a place for environmental education and conservation work. There are no fancy facilities, but it is well worth visiting to teach children about protecting life. Hours, fees and whether releases are possible vary by season, so check with the center before you go.
Once eggs hatch, the hatchlings are usually released into the sea within about a week. One guide says visitors pay about
to release a hatchling themselves. Some days there are no hatchlings, so check ahead.
Volunteers patrolling the beach at night move freshly laid eggs to the center and bury them in fenced sand pits. Only trained volunteers may enter the pits, and the eggs are said to hatch after about
51 days
. Hatchlings that cannot climb out of the pit on their own are not helped, so only healthy ones reach the sand and head for the sea.
A turtle-shaped concrete pool holds hatchlings until they are released. Two adult turtles that cannot be returned to the sea because of injuries caused by people are also said to live here.

A small exhibit hall introduces the turtle life cycle and the threats it faces, and visitors attend a lecture. Much of the content is easy for children to grasp, such as the explanation that the temperature of the sand where eggs are buried decides the sex, with warmer sand producing more females. The hatchery is also shown during the lecture.
The center patrols about
7 km

of shoreline to protect nesting turtles. Guides say applications for night patrol volunteering are accepted year-round, and during the nesting season students from the Philippines and abroad sometimes come to volunteer for nearly a week.

The Bataan tourism office says the Pawikan Festival is held every November. One guide says it takes place in the last week of November, and it is an occasion to showcase release events and conservation activities. Dates can change from year to year, so check the Bataan tourism office announcements.
A quiet, fine-sand beach that is nice for children to play on. Turtles nest here, so do not shine lights at night or touch the turtles.

items.title: Half-day visit
items.subtitle: Arrive in time for a release

children.text: Take a bus bound for Balanga from Pasay or Cubao in Manila.
Arrive in Balanga, have a light breakfast and transfer to a bus bound for Morong.
Travel from Morong to the Nagbalayong coast. The last stretch is sandy, so check the tricycle or vehicle situation.
Pay the entrance fee at the center and attend the lecture. Look around the hatchery and the turtle pool.
Ask staff whether there are hatchlings to release, then take part in a release on the beach.
Have lunch in Morong or Balanga and head back.
Releases are only possible when hatchlings are available. Your chances are best between November and February, the nesting and hatching season.

items.title: Together with the nuclear plant tour
items.subtitle: A one-day west Bataan route

children.text: Finish your pre-booked tour of the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant.
Have lunch in Morong town.
Arrive at the Pawikan Conservation Center, attend the lecture and see the hatchery.
If a release is possible, go out to the beach.
Head back before dark.
The two sites are in the same Nagbalayong coastal area, so they are easy to combine in one trip.
A bus bound for Balanga from Cubao or Pasay costs about
(based on visitor reports).
From Balanga, a bus to Morong costs about
, and visitors report that buses run until around 8 p.m.
Morong is about
51 km
from Balanga and about
175 km
from Manila.
The route described runs west from Balanga through Pilar and Bagac and then north along the coast. It is easy to overshoot near Anvaya Cove.
Directions say to leave the highway toward the sea, turning left when coming from Morong and right when coming from Subic or Anvaya Cove.
Visitors report that the last stretch turns into a sandy road between houses where ordinary cars can get stuck. Look for the "Bantay Pawikan, Inc." signs.
From Morong town to the beach you can use a tricycle. Bargain over the fare.
Hiring a taxi or chartered vehicle makes it easy to combine the center with the nuclear plant tour.
Releases are described as being done by staff carrying the hatchlings in containers to the water's edge.
The center's address is given as Purok VI-Aplaya, Nagbalayong, Morong. Map apps may be inaccurate about the location, so ask locals to confirm.

Conservation work is busiest during the nesting season. The Bataan tourism office gives the nesting season as September to January, one guide names November to February as the busiest period, and one travel account says eggs appear from August to February. The ranges differ by source, so check the exact timing with the center.

Releases are only possible on days when hatchlings have emerged, so your best chance is between late autumn and early spring. Student volunteers from across the country and abroad also gather in this period.

In the June–October rainy season, rain and typhoons can make the coastal road difficult. Outside the nesting season a release may not be possible, but you can still see the exhibit and the center. Guides say the center is open daily from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., though this may vary by season.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Guides mention rooms near the center that sleep up to about 15 people for about
per night. They suit groups or families who want to stay and volunteer. Most visitors stay in Balanga and make a day trip.

It is safest to eat first in Balanga or Morong town. Arcee's Restaurant in Balanga is often mentioned as a lunch stop on this route. Small restaurants in the beach villages also serve grilled fish and Filipino home cooking.
Morong itself is a quiet coastal town and few restaurants are open at night. If you plan to stay into the evening, bring food or return to Balanga for dinner.
If you want to see a release, contact the center in advance to confirm there are hatchlings. Check local notices for contact details.
Reservations are not required, but arrive early so you do not miss the release time.
The sun is strong, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Explain to children beforehand that they must not touch or carry the turtles around before a release.
Do not use flash on hatchlings when taking photos.
If you want to volunteer or donate, ask on site. Guides say night patrol volunteers are accepted year-round.
Do not leave trash on the beach and follow Leave No Trace principles.
For a day trip from Manila, leaving early in the morning makes it much easier.
Visitors report that the center is open daily from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., but releases depend on when the hatchlings emerge, so arriving early is safest.
Turtles come ashore to nest at Nagbalayong and nearby beaches, so if you go out on the beach at night, do not shine lights and follow the center's instructions.

Official fee and opening-hour notices for this center are hard to find, and the numbers differ between visitor reports. The entrance fee, release fee and contact details come from past sources, so be sure to check before you visit.
Hatchlings are fragile, so do not touch or move them on your own, and follow the staff's instructions.
Shining lights or making noise on the beach at night disturbs turtles coming ashore to nest.
Outside the release season there may be no hatchlings, so check with the center before you visit.
The coastal road has sand, so it can be slippery in the rain and cars can get stuck.
Birds of prey sometimes snatch hatchlings on their way to the sea, so do not shout or rush at them while watching.
A nuclear plant on the same Nagbalayong coast that was never put into operation. Tours are possible by advance booking.
A resort in Bagac with restored Spanish colonial-era houses, easy to combine with a west coast route.
The Subic Bay Freeport area north of Morong, with sea and forest activities.
The provincial capital of Bataan, a base town with lodging and restaurants.
